This volume re-evaluates some of the major interventions in the development of modern education in India since the mid-nineteenth century. The empirically rich essays focus on the initiatives to promote education among the socially and educationally backward Dalit communities and the status of Dalit institutions. The authors argue forcefully about the centrality of education in fostering social mobility and change. The essays on women’s education discuss how intensely controversial it was to educate girls, and how women struggled to establish their identity and make their voices heard in a traditional society undergoing a transition to modernity.

Saurav Kumar Rai, Research Officer, Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti, New Delhi

Ayurveda, Nation and Society captures the late nineteenth and early twentieth century growth of the Ayurvedic revivalist movement and ‘medical nationalism’ in the United Provinces. Critiquing the casteist, communal, class-based and patriarchal notions undergirding the Ayurvedic discourse of the period, the author argues that the proponents of Ayurveda were actively reconstructing not only a tradition but also a society and ‘nation’. The book also uses hitherto untapped sources to study the commercialisation of the health discourse and demonstrates how, despite co-opting several traits of Western medicine, Ayurvedic practitioners have often ignored one of its central tenets—the spirit of rigorous enquiry.

Contents: Introduction; 1. Ayurveda as ‘Indigenous’ Medicine: Historical Backdrop and Complexities 2. Indian National Congress and the Late Colonial Ayurvedic Movement 3. Creating an Ayurvedic Discourse: Print, Organisation and Mobilisation 4. Healing the Society: Social Culture of the Late Colonial Ayurvedic Discourse 5. cases.question: Who wrote A Critical History of Women's Health in Modern Sri Lanka?
cases.answer: A Critical History of Women's Health in Modern Sri Lanka was written by Darshi Thoradeniya.

retrieved.text:
Critical History of Women’s Health in Modern Sri Lanka, A

series: new perspectives in south asian history

Darshi Thoradeniya, Senior Lecturer, Department of History, University of Colombo

How have individual women’s bodies fared within the twentieth-century Sri Lankan stories of development? In A Critical History of Women’s Health in Modern Sri Lanka, Darshi Thoradeniya traces women’s health in Sri Lanka from the initial days of birth control and family planning, to development and population control, to the militarisation and financialisation of women’s bodies. Questioning this ‘success story’, she shows, through meticulous research, interviews, policies and advertisements, and oral narratives, how women’s bodies were used for the nation-building project of post-independence Sri Lanka while individual women’s unique bodily and medical experiences were silenced.

20 HISTORY

S. W. D. Bandaranaike. Since then, Sri Lanka has been consistently held as a model of good health at low cost.

This book explores the implementation of primary healthcare in Sri Lanka against the background of a 30-year internal conflict. It includes an analysis of how international health organisations like the WHO imposed a global health agenda on the developing world through a study of a joint WHO–Sri Lanka project on tuberculosis control. Ayurveda, Nation and Society captures the late nineteenth and early twentieth century growth of the Ayurvedic revivalist movement and ‘medical nationalism’ in the United Provinces. Critiquing the casteist, communal, class-based and patriarchal notions undergirding the Ayurvedic discourse of the period, the author argues that the proponents of Ayurveda were actively reconstructing not only a tradition but also a society and ‘nation’. The book also uses hitherto untapped sources to study the commercialisation of the health discourse and demonstrates how, despite co-opting several traits of Western medicine, Ayurvedic practitioners have often ignored one of its central tenets—the spirit of rigorous enquiry.

This definitive collection of essays, divided into five sections, depicts James Manor’s wide range of interests. The first section is a commentary on the emergence of a consolidated democracy in India, and discusses two major themes– political awakening and political decay–which, together with political regeneration, forms the three key processes at work in Indian politics over the past forty years. He devotes three sections to the nature of political parties, the trends of regional politics, and how, at all these levels, political actors manage the challenges of governance. He addresses the regional dynamics of politics through the lens of political leadership in the fourth section, and in the last, comments on the more recent phase of Indian politics.
